My interests are in engineering and aerospace as well, as I've done much of my research in this area. I've attended and participated in numerous hackathons in the past and won a few. My friends and I have hosted our own recently. I would love to partner with students who share some of my interests as well, and I wish the best for everyone.
summary:
LUNARIS is a web tool that answers the following question for any lunar south pole landing site: will the Sun and Earth be above the local horizon, and for how long will this occur? A user picks one of 10 curated sites or enters coordinates, sets a landing time, and compares up to four site-date scenarios on a shared clock across the entire site. Each card shows countdowns to the next sunset and Earthset, sunlit and Earth-visible percentages, and plain good, marginal, or poor verdicts for power and communications.

LUNARIS traces horizons over NASA LOLA terrain on a curved Moon using SPICE DE440 ephemerides, with the Sun and Earth treated as finite discs. Sun positions match JPL Horizons to about 1e-8 degrees, and repeating this evaluation on 100 published terrain variants will report how much the overall results have spread with terrain uncertainty. A precomputed static demo runs in any browser without a backend. We have also included advanced workspace extensions for transfer, descent, and touchdown simulation. 

At the pole, the Sun stays within a few degrees of the horizon, meaning that one ridge or one day can lead to days of darkness. Comparison against NASA illumination maps is still open to ensure our results are scientifically accurate to the published data.
details:
LUNARIS is a web tool that answers one question for any lunar south pole landing site: will the Sun and Earth be above the local horizon, and for how long? A user picks one of 10 curated sites or enters coordinates, sets a landing time and a window of 3 days, 14 days, or one lunar day, and compares up to four site-date scenarios on a shared clock. Each card shows countdowns to the next sunset and Earthset, sunlit and Earth-visible percentages, longest darkness, and plain good, marginal, or poor verdicts for power and communications. The website sends each request to a Python backend built with FastAPI, which runs the calculations as background jobs with progress updates and caching, so repeated scenarios return quickly. Results are saved as revisions in SQLite, and the frontend (React, TypeScript, three.js, and d3) displays them. A precomputed static demo covering 1 December 2026 to 30 January 2027 runs in any browser without a backend, using the same engine and slicing code as live mode.

For the physics, LUNARIS uses NASA’s SPICE toolkit with the DE440 ephemeris, a very precise table of where the Sun, Earth, and Moon are at any moment, along with reference frames that match the Moon’s real orientation. To find the skyline, we use NASA LOLA elevation maps (5 m detail near each site and 240 m across the wider region) and trace rays outward from the lander in 1,440 compass directions, out to 300 km over a curved Moon. This records how high the terrain rises in each direction for a panel or antenna 2 m above the ground. The Sun and Earth are treated as finite discs instead of points, so we calculate how much of each disc is above the skyline and count a body as up once more than 1% of it is visible. This also captures Earth blocking part of the Sun. Exact rise and set times come from Brent’s method, a root-finding algorithm that closes in on the moment a body crosses the skyline, down to 0.125 seconds. Solar power is 1361 W/m² adjusted for distance from the Sun, multiplied by panel area, efficiency, the cosine of the angle between the sunlight and the panel, and the visible disc fraction, then added up over time into a battery charge. For communications, we check line of sight to Earth and run a link budget to three 34 m Deep Space Network stations. A link budget is an accounting of how much signal strength survives the trip, covering distance loss, antenna gain, noise, and a 10° minimum station elevation.

Because terrain data is never perfect, we repeat the same evaluation on all 100 terrain variants NASA published for Site01 and report the results as percentile spreads, which show how much an answer can shift with terrain uncertainty. We checked our work against outside tools. Our Sun positions match JPL Horizons to about 1e-8 degrees, four trajectory cases match NASA’s GMAT, a second gravity implementation agrees to 2e-7 m, and independent recomputations matched our link budget at 222.63 dB path loss at 8.4 GHz. We have also included an advanced workspace that continues past site screening into mission design. It uses Lambert targeting (finding the transfer orbit between two points in a set time), an adaptive ODE solver called DOP853, Kalman filters for navigation, and a 6-degree-of-freedom descent simulation with landing legs. At the pole, the Sun stays within a few degrees of the horizon, so one ridge or one day can lead to days of darkness. Our good, marginal, and poor thresholds are illustrative, and the comparison against NASA illumination maps is still open, so the app labels both clearly.
